# Understanding Cairns: A Summary

## Core Concept
A cairn is a pile of marks with a measurable height. Various operations can change its height in predictable ways.

## The Pulse (Rule C1)
When you pulse a cairn, it grows by two components:
1. The stride (a fixed unit of measurement)
2. A bonus equal to how many complete stride-sized chunks fit into the current height

The key insight: you always count fresh from the current height. The formula is: New height = Current height + stride + (current height ÷ stride, rounded down).

## Multiple Pulses (Rule C2)
Each successive pulse must recalculate the full stride count from the new height. You cannot reuse previous calculations. The cairn grows faster and faster because it gets taller after each pulse, allowing more strides to fit.

## The Leak (Rule C3)
A leak removes marks after a pulse happens. The amount lost equals how many complete "leak-sized chunks" fit into the height immediately after pulsing. The leak is applied to the post-pulse height, not before.

## Finding the Origin (Rule C4)
To work backwards from a final height to discover the starting height, you must undo each pulse by finding what height would produce that result when pulsed. This is not simple subtraction—you must reverse-engineer by testing values.

## The Drain (Rule C5)
A drain removes a fixed number of marks each cycle after pulsing. Unlike a leak, the drain amount never changes. A cairn only empties if the drain exceeds what a pulse adds (which varies based on current height).

## Merging (Rule C6)
Two cairns combine using: weighted portions from each cairn (based on shares in tenths) plus a tether value scaled to the shorter cairn's size. The formula: floor(w × q1) + floor((1-w) × q2) + (tether contribution).
